concept.title: WPA2 vs WPA3
concept.shortdesc: WPA2 and WPA3 are security protocols that protect wireless networks. WPA3 provides stronger security than WPA2, but all connected devices must support the selected security mode.

section.title: Overview
section.p: Wi-Fi Protected Access (WPA) protocols control access to a wireless network and protect data sent between wireless devices and the access point.
WPA2 is widely supported by older and current devices. WPA3 provides improved authentication and stronger protection against password-guessing attempts.
section.note: Use WPA3 when the router and all client devices support it. Use WPA2 only when a device cannot connect through WPA3.

section.title: WPA2
section.p: WPA2 is a wireless security protocol that uses authentication and encryption to protect a Wi-Fi network.
WPA2 is compatible with many computers, mobile devices, printers, smart TVs, and IoT devices. This broad compatibility can make WPA2 necessary for networks that include older devices.
section.note: If you use WPA2, select WPA2 with AES encryption. Do not use obsolete protocols or encryption methods such as WEP or TKIP.
WPA2-Personal uses a pre-shared key to authenticate devices. The security of the network depends on the strength and confidentiality of the Wi-Fi password.

section.title: WPA3
section.p: WPA3 is a newer wireless security protocol. It improves the authentication process and provides increased protection against password-guessing attempts.
The supports . Use this mode when all required client devices support WPA3.
section.note: WPA3-Personal uses Simultaneous Authentication of Equals (SAE) instead of the WPA2-Personal pre-shared key authentication process. SAE provides increased resistance to offline password guessing.
WPA3 requires Protected Management Frames (PMF). PMF protects specified wireless management frames against forgery and some disconnection attacks.

section.title: WPA2/WPA3 Transition Mode
section.p: A WPA2/WPA3 transition mode permits WPA2 and WPA3 devices to connect to the same Wi-Fi network. Use this mode when the network contains both older and newer devices.
WPA3-compatible devices use WPA3. Devices that do not support WPA3 can use WPA2.
section.note: Transition mode provides compatibility, but it permits devices to use the less secure WPA2 protocol. Use WPA3-only mode when all required devices support WPA3.
Test all client devices before you change from transition mode to WPA3-only mode. Older IoT devices, printers, and media devices might not support WPA3.

section.title: Recommended Security Mode
section.p: Set the to when all required devices support WPA3.
If a required device does not support WPA3, use WPA2/WPA3 transition mode. Use WPA2 with AES only when transition mode is not available.
section.note: A strong security protocol does not replace a strong password. Create a long and unique for the wireless network.
